It is sometimes applied to everything that makes a sound, by likening or by extension, as in their saying "the dove spoke (naṭaqat)"; and from it come "the speaking and the silent" for animals and inanimate things. For animal sounds, inasmuch as they follow imaginings, are given the status of expressions, especially as some of them vary with the variation of purposes, so that those of their own kind understand them.»
Al-Zamakhsharī added to what al-Bayḍāwī said: «Yaʿqūb ibn al-Sikkīt entitled his book Iṣlāḥ al-Manṭiq (The Correction of Speech), and he corrected in it nothing but single words.»
It appears that the etymological origin of the word «المنطق» shows us the close connection between thought and language: the thinking animal alone is the speaking animal. Language is not merely a tool that the human mind has fashioned to express its purposes and aims; it is also a means of abstracting from sensory accidents and fashioning certain symbols or abstract significations.
The science of logic (ʿilm al-manṭiq) is a science that investigates sound and corrupt thinking. It lays down the rules that protect the mind from falling into errors in judgments, and it is also concerned with knowing the various methods [of scholars] in their many studies and diverse researches. It is true that the subject of logic is human thinking in general, but logic is not limited to describing the mental operations we perform when we think, judge, abstract, remember or solve a problem; it also seeks to help us distinguish between the correct judgment and the mistaken one, between sound inference and corrupt inference.
The ancient Greek philosophers were concerned with studying the relationship between the form of thought and its matter, i.e., between the formal aspect of judgments or propositions and the content of thinking itself; from that arose dialectical inquiries which were the first nucleus of the science of logic. Thus Socrates and Plato were concerned with investigating the fallacies of the Sophists, and to refute them they laid down the principles of sound dialectical thinking. Then came Aristotle, who benefited from the studies of those before him in forming concepts, logical division and the methods of presenting proof, and he put all this into a famous book called "the Prior Analytics". And although Aristotle did not use the word "logic", the historians agree in pledging allegiance to him as the prince of logic.
In modern times, both Bacon and Descartes rebelled against Aristotle's logic, claiming that it is a barren formal logic. Then the logicians finally realized the necessity of freeing thought from the magic of words and liberating it from the authority of language, and they tried to make logic a mathematical science that formulates mental operations in algebraic symbols.
(يُوزَعُونَ): the first of them are held back for the last of them, i.e., the vanguard (sullāf) of the army is halted until those following catch up with them; «سلاف العسكر» means their foremost, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. In al-Mukhtār: «وزعه يزعه وزعا, like وضعه يضعه وضعا, i.e., he restrained him, and اتّزع, i.e., he refrained. أوزعه بالشيء: he incited him to it. استوزعت الله شكره فأوزعني: I asked Allah to inspire me to thank Him, and He inspired me. Al-wāziʿ is the one who goes ahead of the rank and sets it in order, moving some forward and some back; its plural is wazaʿa. Al-Ḥasan said: "People must have a wāziʿ", i.e., an authority that restrains them. One says وزعت الجيش when you hold back the first of the army for the last of it.»
(نَمْلَةٌ): «النمل» and «النمُل» (with ḍamma on the mīm): a creature eager to gather food; it makes villages under the ground in which there are dwellings, corridors, chambers and winding storeys which it fills with grain and provisions for the winter. The singular is «نملة» and «نمُلة», for male and female, and the plural is «نمال».
Al-Zamakhsharī related of Abū Ḥanīfa that he stood by Qatāda while he was saying: "Ask me." Abū Ḥanīfa ordered a person to ask Qatāda about Solomon's ant: was it male or female? He did not answer. Abū Ḥanīfa was asked about that and said: "It was female," and he argued from the attachment of the marker [of the feminine]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: «That is because «النملة» is like «الحمامة» and «الشاة» in applying to the male and the female, and they are distinguished by a marker, as in "a male dove" and "a female dove".»
[Translator's note: what follows appears to be a quotation of an objection to this report (it resembles the words of Abū Ḥayyān/Ibn al-Munayyir), though the source does not mark it as such.] I do not know which to marvel at more: him, or Abū Ḥanīfa, that this should be established as coming from him. For «النملة», like «الحمامة» and «الشاة», applies to the male and the female, because it is a generic noun: one says «نملة ذكر» and «نملة أنثى» as one says «حمامة ذكر» and «حمامة أنثى», «شاة ذكر» and «شاة أنثى». Its word is feminine and its meaning is open, so it may be treated as feminine for the sake of its word even though it applies to a male; indeed this is the eloquent, current usage. Do you not see his words, upon him be blessings and peace: "No one-eyed, emaciated or blind [animal] is to be sacrificed" — how he put these adjectives in the feminine according to the word, without meaning the females of livestock specifically? So in the words of the Exalted «نملة», the femininity of the word was observed, while the meaning is equally open [to both]. More of this discussion will come in the Benefits section.
(أَوْزِعْنِي): inspire me. Its literal sense is: make me restrain (azaʿu) gratitude for Your favour to me, hold it back and tie it fast, so that it does not escape me, so that I never cease to be grateful to You. The explanation of this root has preceded.

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنا داوُدَ وَسُلَيْمانَ عِلْماً): the wāw is resumptive, and the speech is resumptive, to begin the second story, the story of David and Solomon. The lām paves the way for the oath (muwaṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam); «قد» is a particle of realization; «آتينا» is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); «داود» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), «سليمان» is conjoined to «داود», and «علما» is a second direct object.
(وَقالا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَضَّلَنا عَلى كَثِيرٍ مِنْ عِبادِهِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ): the wāw is a conjunction, and «قالا» is conjoined to something implied, its implied form being: "so they acted upon what they were given, with the heart by resolve, with the limbs by practice, and with the tongue, and they said". «الحمد» is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and «لله» its khabar (predicate), and the clause is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). «الذي» is a relative noun, an adjective of «الله»; the clause «فضلنا» is the ṣila (relative clause); «على كثير» are attached to (mutaʿalliq) «فضلنا»; «من عباده» is an adjective of «كثير», and «المؤمنين» an adjective of «عباده».
(وَوَرِثَ سُلَيْمانُ داوُدَ وَقالَ يا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ عُلِّمْنا مَنْطِقَ الطَّيْرِ): the wāw is resumptive; «ورث سليمان داود» is a verb, its agent and its direct object; «قال» is conjoined to «ورث»; the i'rab of «يا أيها الناس» has preceded. «علمنا» is a passive past verb, «نا» is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent), and «منطق الطير» is a second direct object.
(وَأُوتِينا مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ إِنَّ هذا لَهُوَ الْفَضْلُ الْمُبِينُ): «أوتينا» is conjoined to «علمنا»; «من كل شيء» are attached to «أوتينا». «إن هذا»: «إن» and its noun — it is resumptive speech, brought by way of expressing thanks and praise. The lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); «هو» is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl) or a mubtadaʾ; «الفضل» is the khabar of «إن» or the khabar of «هو», the clause being the khabar of «إن»; and «المبين» is an adjective of «الفضل».
(وَحُشِرَ لِسُلَيْمانَ جُنُودُهُ مِنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنْسِ وَالطَّيْرِ فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ): the wāw is resumptive; «حشر» is a passive past verb; «لسليمان» are attached to «حشر»; «جنوده» is the deputy agent; «من الجن والإنس والطير» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of «جنوده». The fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa; «هم» is a mubtadaʾ and the clause «يوزعون» its khabar. What history relates about Solomon's camp will come in the Rhetoric section.
(حَتَّى إِذا أَتَوْا عَلى وادِ النَّمْلِ قالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يا أَيُّهَا النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَساكِنَكُمْ): «حتى» is a particle of limit for something omitted, its implied form being "so they went on until, when they came…". It may also be the limit of «يوزعون», because it includes the sense of "they travel, some of them prevented from separating from others, until when they came…". «على وادي النمل» is a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to «أتوا»; the secret of attaching it to «أتوا» will come in the Rhetoric section. The clause «قالت نملة» has no grammatical position; the i'rab of «يا أيها النمل» has preceded. «ادخلوا مساكنكم» is a verb, its agent and its direct object by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa). What al-Suyūṭī said in al-Itqān about the ant's words will come.
(لا يَحْطِمَنَّكُمْ سُلَيْمانُ وَجُنُودُهُ وَهُمْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ): a resumptive prohibition with no connection to what precedes it, i.e., "do not be where they would crush you". The speech may also be a badal (substitute) of the command clause similar to it, namely «ادخلوا مساكنكم».
Al-Zamakhsharī addressed this expression and said: «If you say: what is «لا يحطمنكم»? I say: it may be a reply to the command, or a prohibition that is a badal of the command. What permits it to be a badal of it is that it carries the sense of "do not be where you are, so that he crushes you", in the manner [Translator's note: the source prints «طريقه», evidently for «طريقة»] of «لا أرينك هاهنا» (let me not see you here).» «لا» is the prohibitive lā; «يحطمنكم» is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa, in the position of jussive by «لا»; the kāf is the direct object; «سليمان» is the agent and «جنوده» is conjoined to «سليمان». «وهم»: the wāw is of ḥāl, «هم» a mubtadaʾ and the clause «لا يشعرون» its khabar, and the clause is a ḥāl.
(فَتَبَسَّمَ ضاحِكاً مِنْ قَوْلِها): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted that the context requires, i.e., "so he heard her aforementioned words and smiled". «ضاحكا» is an emphasizing ḥāl (ḥāl muʾakkida); the secret of what made him laugh will come in the Benefits section. «من قولها» are attached to «ضاحكا».
(وَقالَ رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ وَعَلى والِدَيَّ): «قال» is conjoined to «فتبسم». «رب» is one addressed (munādā), annexed to the yāʾ of the speaker, which is omitted, and the vocative particle is omitted. «أوزعني» is a verb of supplication, a latent (mustatir) agent and a direct object. «أن» with what falls in its scope is the second object of «أوزعني», because it includes the sense of inspiring; or it is accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., «بأن أشكر نعمتك». «التي» is an adjective of «نعمتك»; the clause «أنعمت» is the ṣila; «عليّ» are attached to «أنعمت», and «على والدي» is conjoined to «عليّ».
(وَأَنْ أَعْمَلَ صالِحاً تَرْضاهُ): a conjoined clause.
(وَأَدْخِلْنِي بِرَحْمَتِكَ فِي عِبادِكَ الصَّالِحِينَ): the wāw is a conjunction; «أدخلني» is a verb of supplication, its agent and its direct object; «برحمتك» are attached to an omitted ḥāl, the bāʾ being causal; «في عبادك» are attached to «أدخلني», and «الصالحين» is a naʿt (adjective) of «عبادك».

* Rhetoric:
These verses contain various arts, which we set out below:
1- Indefiniteness and its secrets:
In His words «وقد آتينا داود وسليمان علما» [Translator's note: so in the source; the verse reads «ولقد»] there is indefiniteness, whose benefit is to convey partiality and paucity, or to convey magnification and abundance; the second is what is meant here. The apparent sense of His words «ولقد آتينا داود وسليمان علما», in the context of conferring favour, is the magnification of the knowledge they were given, as if He said: knowledge — and what knowledge! And so it was, for their knowledge was of a kind found strange and great, including knowledge of the speech of birds and of the other animals; although every knowledge, compared with the knowledge of Allah, is little and slight.
A wonderful story:
We give here a related story, following our custom of including related stories so that they may be a source of inspiration for writers and landmarks of daylight for them. Muqātil said: Solomon was sitting in his camp, whose area was a hundred parasangs by a hundred: twenty-five for the jinn, twenty-five for humans, twenty-five for the birds and twenty-five for the wild beasts. The jinn had woven for him a carpet of gold and silk, a parasang by a parasang. A bird passed by him circling — and in one report he saw a nightingale on a tree — and he said to those sitting with him: "Do you know what this bird says?" They said: "Allah and His Prophet know best." He said: "It says: I have eaten half a date, so may the world perish." He passed by a hoopoe on top of a tree and said: "[It says:] Ask Allah's forgiveness, O sinners." A ring-dove cried, and he told them that it says: "Would that these creatures had not been created." A peacock cried, and he said it says: "As you judge, so shall you be judged." A ṭīṭawā [a sandpiper-like bird] cried, and he said it says: "Every living thing will die, and every new thing will wear out." A swallow cried, and he said it says: "Send forward good and you will find it." A turtle-dove cried, and he told them that it says: "Glory be to my Lord the Most High." He said: the kite says: "Everything perishes except His Face"; the sandgrouse says: "Whoever keeps silent is safe"; the parrot says: "Woe to the one whose concern is the world"; the cock says: "Remember Allah, O heedless ones"; the vulture says: "O son of Adam, live as long as you will; your end is death"; the eagle says: "In distance from people there is companionship [with Allah]"; and the frog says: "Glory be to my Lord the Most High."
2- The use of the preposition:
He said «حتى إذا أتوا على وادي النمل», making «أتوا» transitive with «على», because the coming was from above, so He used the particle of superiority (istiʿlāʾ). Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī glimpsed this lofty sky and said:
فلشد ما جاوزت قدرك صاعد ... ولشدّ ما قربت عليك الأنجم
(How far you have overstepped your worth, climbing! How near the stars have come to you!)
By "the stars" he meant the verses of his poetry. He says: how greatly you have overstepped your worth, sending to ask me for praise! Your asking me to praise you is an overstepping of your worth on your part, since you sought that the stars descend from their heavens to come near you. This verse is among the most stinging and foul-mouthed of satire. It is from an ode by Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī [Translator's note: the source prints «المتبني» here]. He had travelled from al-Ramla intending Antioch and stopped at Tripoli, where Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Aʿwar ibn Kayghalagh was; he was ignorant, and three men of the Banū Ḥaydara used to sit with him, between whom and Abū al-Ṭayyib there was an old enmity. They said to him: "Would you like him to pass you by and not praise you?" and they kept inciting him. So he sent to him asking that he praise him, and Abū al-Ṭayyib excused himself by an oath binding him not to praise anyone for a period. So he held him back from his journey to wait out the period, and took the road from him and controlled it. The three men who had been inciting him died within forty days. Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī then satirized him and dictated the poem to someone he trusted. When the snow melted, he went out as if exercising his horse and travelled to Damascus. Ibn Kayghalagh sent horsemen and footmen after him, but he escaped them, and the ode became known. Its beginning is:
لهوى النفوس سريرة لا تعلم ... عرضا نظرت وخلت أني أسلم
(The passion of souls has a secret that is not known; I glanced by chance and thought I would be safe.)
Among its verses of wisdom:
ولقد رأيت الحادثات فلا أرى ... يققا يميت ولا سوادا يعصم
(I have seen the events of fortune, and I see neither white hair that kills nor black hair that protects.)
والهم يخترم الجسيم نحافة ... ويشيب ناصية الصبيّ ويهرم
(Worry wastes the stout body into leanness, whitens the forelock of the boy and makes him old.)
ذو العقل يشقى في النعيم بعقله ... وأخو الجهالة في الشقاوة ينعم
(The man of intelligence is wretched amid bliss because of his intelligence, while the brother of ignorance lives in comfort amid wretchedness.)
والناس قد نبذوا الحفاظ فمطلق ... ينسى الذي يولى وعاف يندم
(People have cast off loyalty: the one released forgets the favour done him, and the one who pardons regrets it.)
لا يخدعنّك من عدوّ دمعه ... وارحم شبابك من عدوّ ترحم
(Let not an enemy's tear deceive you; have mercy on your youth from an enemy you pity.)
لا يسلم الشرف الرفيع من الأذى ... حتّى يراق على جوانبه الدّم
(Lofty honour is not safe from harm until blood is shed around it.)
والظلم من شيم النفوس فإن تجد ... داعفة فلعلّة لا يظلم
(Injustice is part of the nature of souls; if you find one who is chaste, it is for some reason that he does not do wrong.) [Translator's note: the source prints «داعفة»; the familiar text is «ذا عفة».]
Then he turned to satirizing Ibn Kayghalagh, and was foul-mouthed:
يحمي ابن كيغلغ الطريق وعرسه ... ما بين رجليها الطريق الأعظم
(Ibn Kayghalagh guards the road, while his wife… [an obscene insult about her unchastity].)
أقم المسالح وق شفر سكينة ... إن المنيّ بحلقتيها خضرم
(Station your guards over Sukayna's [obscene sexual insult].) [Translator's note: the source prints «وق», evidently for «فوق».]
وارفق بنفسك إنّ خلقك ناقص ... واستر أباك فإنّ أصلك مظلم
(Go easy on yourself, for your make is deficient; and hide your father, for your origin is dark.)
واحذر مناوأة الرجال فإنما ... تقوى على كسر العبيد وتقدم
(Beware of contending with men, for you are only strong and bold enough to break slaves.)
وغناك مسألة وطيشك نفخة ... ورضاك فيشلة وربك درهم
(Your wealth is from begging, your rashness mere bluster, your satisfaction [an obscene word], and your lord a dirham.)
Then he returns to fitting wisdom, saying:
ومن البلية عذل من لا يرعوي ... عن غيّه وخطاب من لا يفهم
(It is an affliction to reproach one who will not desist from his error, and to address one who does not understand.)
[Translator's note: from here the lines are broken across lines in the source; they are given as whole verses with the text unchanged.]
يمشي بأربعة على أعقابه ... تحت العلوج ومن وراء يلجم
(He walks on all fours backwards beneath the louts, and is bridled from behind.)
وجفونه ما تستقر كأنها ... مطروفة أو فتّ فيها حصرم
(His eyelids never stay still, as if they had been struck in the eye or sour grapes crumbled into them.)
وإذا أشار محدثا فكأنه ... قرد يقهقه أو عجوز تلصم
(When he gestures while talking, it is as if he were a cackling ape or an old woman slapping [her face].) [Translator's note: «تلصم» is as printed; the familiar text is «تلطم».]
يقلى مفارقة الأكفّ قذاله ... حتى يكاد على يد يتعمّم
(His nape hates to be parted from slapping hands, so much that he almost wears a turban of hands.)
وتراه أصغر ما تراه ناطقا ... ويكون أكذب ما يكون ويقسم
(You see him at his smallest when speaking, and he is at his most lying when he swears.)
والذل يظهر في الذليل مودة ... وأودّ منه لمن يودّ الأرقم
(Abasement shows itself in the abased as affection; but the speckled viper is more loving than he to one who loves it.)
ومن العداوة ما ينالك نفعه ... ومن الصداقة ما يضر ويؤلم
(There is enmity whose benefit reaches you, and friendship that harms and hurts.)
The whole ode is of this splendid kind; what we have given of it suffices us. Returning to what we were dealing with, we say: it may also mean crossing the valley and reaching its end, from their saying «أتى على الشيء» when one reaches its end.
3- Tawlīd (generation of figures):
The verse «قالت نملة يا أيها النمل ادخلوا مساكنكم لا يحطمنكم سليمان وجنوده وهم لا يشعرون» contains eleven kinds of rhetoric, some generated from others, which al-Suyūṭī mentioned in his book al-Itqān. That is, she spoke words containing letters and sounds, and what is meant is that she said it by way of good counsel; and these words of hers contained eleven kinds of rhetoric:
First: the call with «يا».
Second: she used an indirect designation with «أي».
Third: she gave notice with the hāʾ of alerting (hāʾ al-tanbīh).
Fourth: she named, by saying «النمل».
Fifth: she commanded, by saying «ادخلوا».
Sixth: she specified, by saying «مساكنهم» [Translator's note: so in the source; the verse reads «مساكنكم»].
Seventh: she warned, by saying «لا يحطمنكم».
Eighth: she particularized, by saying «سليمان».
Ninth: she generalized, by saying «وجنوده».
Tenth: she pointed, by saying «وهم».
Eleventh: she excused, by saying «لا يشعرون».
They also recited, posing a riddle about Solomon's ant and the cow of the Children of Israel:
فما ميت أحيا له الله ميتا ... ليخبر قوما أنذروا ببيان
(What dead thing was it for whose sake Allah brought a dead man to life, to inform a people who were warned plainly?)
وعجفاء قد قامت لتنذر قومها ... واهل قراها رهبة الحدثان
(And a lean female who rose to warn her people and the folk of her villages for fear of calamity?)

* Benefits:
1- What made Solomon laugh?
Solomon laughed at the ant's words for two reasons:
The first: what indicated the evident mercy of him and his soldiers and their compassion, namely her saying «وهم لا يشعرون», meaning that if they were aware they would not do it.
The second: his joy at what Allah had given him, which He had given no one else: his hearing perceiving what the ant said, though it is proverbial for smallness and insignificance. When a person sees or hears something he has no acquaintance with, he laughs.
2- The explanatory and the emphasizing ḥāl:
The ḥāl is of two kinds: founding (muʾassisa), also called explanatory (mubayyina), whose meaning cannot be obtained without it, as in «جاء زيد راكبا» (Zayd came riding), where the meaning of riding is obtained only by mentioning «راكبا»; and emphasizing (muʾakkida), whose meaning is obtained without mentioning it. The latter is divided into three kinds:
a- Emphasizing its governing word in wording and meaning, as in «وأرسلناك للناس رسولا»: «رسولا» is a ḥāl of the kāf, and it emphasizes its governing word «أرسلنا» in wording and meaning.
b- Emphasizing its governing word in meaning only, the wording being different, as in «فتبسم ضاحكا»: «ضاحكا» is a ḥāl of the agent of «تبسم», and it emphasizes its governing word in meaning only, because smiling is a kind of laughing, while the wording is different.
c- Emphasizing its owner (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl), as in «لآمن من في الأرض كلهم جميعا»: «جميعا» is a ḥāl of the agent of «آمن», namely the relative «من», emphasizing it. There are other kinds of the emphasizing ḥāl, for which the extensive works should be consulted.

dervis-irab:79-82.t:
* I'rab:
(فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ إِنَّكَ عَلَى الْحَقِّ الْمُبِينِ): the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (the fāʾ indicating an implied condition), because it is a consequence drawn from His saying «العزيز العليم», i.e. if you have come to know these attributes of Allah the Exalted and believe in them, then rely. (توكل) is an imperative verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you"; (على الله) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (توكل). The clause (إنك على الحق المبين) has no grammatical position, because it gives the reason for the reliance; (إن), its noun and its khabar (predicate); (المبين) is an adjective. (إِنَّكَ لا تُسْمِعُ الْمَوْتى وَلا تُسْمِعُ الصُّمَّ الدُّعاءَ إِذا وَلَّوْا مُدْبِرِينَ): a second reason for the command to rely; it cuts off his hope of their following him. (إن) and its noun, and the clause (لا تسمع) is the khabar; (الموتى) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (ولا تسمع الصم) is conjoined to the one before it; (الصم) is the first direct object and (الدعاء) the second direct object. (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the meaning of condition; the clause (ولوا) is in the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; (مدبرين) is a ḥāl (circumstantial). (وَما أَنْتَ بِهادِي الْعُمْيِ عَنْ ضَلالَتِهِمْ): the wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is the Ḥijāzī negative that operates like (ليس); (أنت) is its noun; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition, and (هادي) is genitive in wording and accusative in position as the khabar of (ما); (العمي) is muḍāf ilayhi; (عن ضلالتهم) is attached to (هادي), made transitive with (عن) because it contains the meaning of "turning them away". Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted another view, namely that it is attached to (العمي), because you say «عمي عن كذا» ("he was blind to such-and-such"), and it is a permissible, acceptable view. Al-Zamakhsharī illustrated the first view with their saying «سقاه عن العيمة», i.e. he kept him away from it by giving him drink; al-ʿayma is the craving for milk, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (إِنْ تُسْمِعُ إِلَّا مَنْ يُؤْمِنُ بِآياتِنا فَهُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ): (إن) is negative; (تسمع) is an imperfect verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (من) is the direct object, and the clause (يؤمن) is the ṣila (relative clause); (بآياتنا) is attached to (يؤمن); the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa; (هم) is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and (مسلمون) the khabar.
(وَإِذا وَقَعَ الْقَوْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ أَخْرَجْنا لَهُمْ دَابَّةً مِنَ الْأَرْضِ): the wāw is resumptive, and the speech is resumptive, introduced to set out some of the signs of the Hour that point to it. What is meant by "the word" is what the Qur'an has pronounced of the verses that tell of the Hour, and what is meant by its "falling", though it has not yet fallen, is the nearness of its occurrence. (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the meaning of condition; the clause (وقع القول) is in the position of the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; (القول) is the agent of (وقع); (عليهم) is attached to (وقع). The clause (أخرجنا) has no grammatical position, because it is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) of a non-jussive condition; (لهم) is attached to (أخرجنا); (دابة) is the direct object; (من الأرض) is an adjective of (دابة). What has been said about the Beast of the Earth will come in the Benefits section.
(تُكَلِّمُهُمْ أَنَّ النَّاسَ كانُوا بِآياتِنا لا يُوقِنُونَ): the clause (تكلمهم) is a second adjective of (دابة), or a ḥāl of it because it has been qualified. (أن) with fatḥa on the hamza is on the supposition of the bāʾ, i.e. «بأن الناس», and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (تكلمهم); it was read with kasra as resumptive. (أن) and its noun, and the clause (كانوا) is the khabar of (أن); (كان) and its noun; (بآياتنا) is attached to (يوقنون); (لا) is negative, and the clause (لا يوقنون) is the khabar of (كانوا). The speech is either from Allah the Exalted or part of the speech of the Beast. Al-Zamakhsharī chose this latter view, and replied to those who objected that His saying «بآياتنا» disturbs that: that its saying is a report of the saying of Allah the Exalted, or is in the sense of "the signs of our Lord", or that, because of its special relation to Allah and its favour with Him, and its being among His select creatures, it annexed Allah's signs to itself, just as some of a king's intimates say "our horses" and "our lands", when they are only the horses and lands of their master.

* Rhetoric:
In His words «ولا تسمع الصم الدعاء إذا ولوا مدبرين» there is the device of īghāl (pressing beyond), which is that the speaker completes the meaning of his speech before bringing its ending, and when he wishes to bring it, he brings what conveys a meaning additional to the meaning of that speech. The speech ended at His words «ولا تسمع الصم الدعاء», so what is the meaning of His words «ولوا مدبرين»? The answer is that He brought it although mentioning the turning away apparently made it unnecessary; but in reality it did not make it unnecessary, because turning away may be with one side rather than another, as aversion may be. Since He, Glorified is He, reported their turning away to complete the meaning in the situation of being addressed — to deny them the understanding that comes from gesture, for the deaf man understands from gesture what the hearer understands from words — then He, Glorified is He, knew that turning away may be with one side rather than another, as we stated, so it is possible for him to glance with the side with which he did not turn, and so grasp some of the gesture; and what is meant is the negation of all gesture. So the verse-ending «مدبرين» came, so that it is known that the turning away was with all sides, such that what had been facing became turned away, and the one addressed was screened from the addresser, since he became behind him; so the gesture was hidden from his unseen just as his ears were deaf to words, and complete exaggeration was achieved in not making him hear at all. This is a representation (tamthīl) by which the state of these people was represented, coming embedded in the īghāl, and this type of īghāl is called the īghāl of precaution (al-iḥtiyāṭ).
There is another type, namely the īghāl of choice (al-takhyīr), whose example has passed in Sūrat al-Māʾida; we have presented in al-Māʾida sufficient examples of īghāl, and we cite here some samples of it. It is related that when Laylā's brothers learned of Tawba ibn al-Ḥumayyir al-ʿUqaylī's love for her, they vowed to shed his blood and moved away with her, so Tawba said:
وان يمنعوا ليلى وحسن حديثها ... فلن يمنعوا عني البكا والقوافيا
فهلا منعتم إذ منعتم حديثها ... خيالا يوافيني مع الليل هاديا
(If they withhold Laylā and her lovely talk, they will not withhold weeping and rhymes from me. Since you withheld her talk, why did you not withhold a phantom that comes to me with the night, guiding its way?)
The meaning was complete with his words «مع الليل», and when he brought the rhyme he added to that.
And by Abū Tammām:
إن المنازل ساورتها فرقة ... أخلت من الآرام كل كناس
من كل ضاحكة الترائب أرهفت ... إرهاف خوط البانة المياس
(The dwellings were assailed by a parting that emptied every covert of its white gazelles — every one with gleaming breast, made slender as the slenderness of the swaying willow-wand.)
The meaning was complete before he brought the rhyme in the second verse, and when he brought it he added to it. In this fine manner it runs consistently for him, and he says:
فتوح أمير المؤمنين تفتحت ... لهن أزاهير الربا والخمائل
لقد ألبس الله الإمام فضائلا ... وتابع فيها باللها والفواضل
فأضحت عطاياه نوازع شردا ... تسائل في الآفاق عن كل سائل
مواهب جدن الأرض حتى كأنما ... أخذن بآداب السحاب الهواطل
(For the conquests of the Commander of the Faithful the blossoms of the hills and thickets have opened. Allah has clothed the Imam with virtues and followed them with gifts and bounties, so that his gifts became roaming strays, asking in the horizons after every asker — endowments that rained generously on the earth, as if they had taken on the manners of the pouring clouds.)

* Benefits:
The Beast of the Earth:
The Beast of the Earth is al-Jassāsa; its tanwīn and indefiniteness are to make its magnification vague, so as to draw attention to it and turn eyes to awaiting its emergence. Much has been said about it in the lengthy works; it is among the matters of the unseen in which we believe, and its essence and reality do not concern us.

dervis-irab:83-88.t:
* Vocabulary:
(فَوْجاً): al-fawj is the group and the party; its plural is afwāj and fuʾūj, and the plural of the plural afāwij, afāyij and afāwīj. Al-fāʾija is the group, and also the open space between any two elevations of sand or rough ground. Al-Rāghib said in his Mufradāt:
«Al-fawj is the group passing by in haste; it seems this is the original sense, then it was applied even when there is no passing or haste. The plural is afwāj and fuʾūj.»
(يُوزَعُونَ): it has preceded recently in Sūrat al-Naḥl [Translator's note: so in the source; the word occurs earlier in this sūra, al-Naml, verse 17], so renew your acquaintance with it; i.e. the first of them are held back for the last of them so that they catch up with one another.
(داخِرِينَ): humbled. In al-Qāmūs: dakhara al-shakhṣ, like manaʿa and fariḥa, dakhran and dukhūran: he became small and abased; and adkhartuhu, with the alif, for transitivity. The dāl with the khāʾ, as the first and second radicals, convey a particular meaning indicating shrinking, self-abasement, and what the soul recoils from and natures find nauseating. Al-dukh and al-dakh is smoke, which is well known to blind the eyes and irritate them. A Bedouin woman said of her husband, who had grown old and aged:
لاخير في الشيخ إذا ما اجلخّا ... وسال غرب عينيه ولخّا
وكان أكلا قاعدا وشخّا ... تحت رواق البيت يغشى الدّخا
وانثنت الرجل فصارت فخّا ... وصار وصل الغانيات أخّا
(There is no good in an old man when he collapses, the stream of his eyes runs and is bleary, his eating and his pissing are done sitting under the tent's awning, frequenting the smoke; his leg has bent and become a snare, and union with beautiful women has become "ugh!")
The meaning of «يغشى الدخ» is that he frequently goes back and forth to the women at the oven, saying "Feed me". The meaning of ijlakhkha is: he fell down and did not move; and it is said its meaning is: he became bent. Akh, with fatḥa on the hamza, is a word said when groaning; thus said Ibn Durayd, who then said: "I reckon it is post-classical." Al-Ṣāghānī said: to a child, when he is forbidden from doing something dirty, one says ikh, with kasra on the hamza, equivalent to the Persians saying kikh, as if it were a rebuke; and its hamza may be given fatḥa. Dakhdakha al-rajul: the man took short steps in haste; tadakhdakha al-rajul: the man shrank. Dakhasa al-shayʾ fī al-ramād: he put the thing into the ashes and buried it; dukhisa al-ḥāfir: the hoof was afflicted by al-dakhas, which is a swelling in the hoof of a riding animal; and al-dukhas, with ḍamma on the dāl, is a sea creature. Dakhala is well known, and it conveys concealment and shrinking. Dukhila fī ʿaqlihi, in the passive, or in his body, and dakhila, with kasra on the khāʾ, dakhalan with two fatḥas: corruption entered him, so he is madkhūl ʿalayhi. Al-dakhl, with fatḥa on the dāl and sukūn on the khāʾ, is what comes in to you of your wealth for you to store and hide from eyes, and also illness and defect. Al-dakhal, with two fatḥas, is what enters a person of corruption in the mind and body, deception, and defect in lineage. Al-dakhīl is one who enters among a people and claims descent from them though not of them, plural dukhalāʾ; and every foreign word. One says dāʾ dakhīl, i.e. an illness that has entered the depths of the body; and one says "He is of wicked dikhla" — with kasra on the doubled dāl — which is the inner side of his affair. Dakhamahu dakhman: he pushed him roughly. Dakhina al-ṭaʿām wal-laḥm, of the taʿiba pattern: smoke affected them while cooking, and nothing is fouler than its taste then. How many marvels this language has!

* I'rab:
(وَيَوْمَ نَحْشُرُ مِنْ كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ فَوْجاً مِمَّنْ يُكَذِّبُ بِآياتِنا فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ): the wāw is resumptive, and the adverb is attached to something omitted, its implied form being "remember"; it is resumptive speech, introduced to show the conditions of the liars in summary form. The clause (نحشر) is in the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; (من كل أمة) is attached to (نحشر), and (من) here is partitive; (فوجا) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (ممن) is an adjective of (فوجا), and (من) here is explicative (for clarification); the clause (يكذب) is the ṣila (relative clause) of (من). The fāʾ is a conjunction; (هم) is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and the clause (يوزعون) is the khabar (predicate).
(حَتَّى إِذا جاؤُ قالَ أَكَذَّبْتُمْ بِآياتِي وَلَمْ تُحِيطُوا بِها عِلْماً أَمَّا ذا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ): (حتى) is a particle of limit; (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the meaning of condition; the clause (جاءوا) is in the position of the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it, and what (جاءوا) is attached to is omitted, i.e. to the place of reckoning. (قال) is a past verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), referring back to Allah the Exalted. (أكذبتم): the hamza is for rebuking, reproaching interrogation, and (كذبتم) is a verb and its agent; (بآياتي) is attached to (كذبتم). In (ولم) the wāw is circumstantial and (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion [to the past] and jussive; (تحيطوا) is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) by (لم); (بها) is attached to (تحيطوا); (علما) is a tamyīz (specification); the clause is circumstantial, emphasising the disapproval and rebuke and showing the hideousness of the denial based on improvisation and the lack of reflection, insight and verification. (أم) is a conjunction, and here it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿa), so it means (بل); (ما) is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ, and (ذا) is a relative noun, the khabar; or (ماذا) as a whole is an interrogative noun in the position of the accusative, the fronted object of (تعملون). (كنتم): (كان) and its noun, and the clause (تعملون) is its khabar. (وَوَقَعَ الْقَوْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِما ظَلَمُوا فَهُمْ لا يَنْطِقُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (وقع القول) is a verb and its agent; (عليهم) is attached to (وقع), and (بما ظلموا) is also attached to (وقع), i.e. because of their wrongdoing, (ما) being maṣdariyya. The fāʾ is a conjunction; (هم) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (لا ينطقون) is the khabar.
(أَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا جَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِيَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ وَالنَّهارَ مُبْصِراً إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ): the hamza is for affirmative and disapproving interrogation; (لم) is a particle of negation, conversion and jussive; (يروا) is an imperfect verb in the jussive by (لم). The seeing here is mental, not visual; (أن) and what follows it stand in place of the two objects of (يروا). (أن) and its noun, and the clause (جعلنا) is its khabar. The making (al-jaʿl) here, if it is in the sense of creating, not of transforming, is transitive to one object, and (الليل) is the object of (جعلنا). The lām is for causation; (يسكنوا) is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied an after the lām of causation, the sign of its accusative being the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the agent; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (جعلنا) as its reason, so it stands as the mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), but the accusative [without the lām] is not permissible because the agent differs. (فيه) is attached to (يسكنوا); (النهار) is conjoined to (الليل); (مبصرا) is a ḥāl (circumstantial) or a second direct object. (إن) is a particle resembling the verb; (في ذلك) is its fronted khabar; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa) and (آيات) is its postponed noun; (لقوم) is an adjective, and the clause (يؤمنون) is an adjective of (قوم).
(وَيَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ فِي الصُّورِ فَفَزِعَ مَنْ فِي السَّماواتِ وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ): (ويوم) is conjoined to «ويوم نحشر», falling under its ruling, which is the command to remember it. The clause (ينفخ) is in the position of the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is latent, its implied form being "it"; (في الصور) is attached to (ينفخ). (ففزع) is conjoined to (ينفخ); the secret of the expression with the past tense will come in the Rhetoric section. (من) is the agent of (فزع), (في السموات) is the ṣila, and (ومن في الأرض) is conjoined to (من في السموات).
(إِلَّا مَنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ داخِرِينَ): (إلا) is a particle of exception and (من) is the excepted; the clause (شاء الله) is the ṣila. (وكل): the wāw is circumstantial or a conjunction; (كل) is a mubtadaʾ, beginning with it being permitted because of the meaning of generality in it and because its tanwīn is a substitute for the muḍāf ilayhi, i.e. "and all of them, after their being brought to life on the Day of Resurrection". The clause (أتوه) is the khabar; the future is expressed with the past because its occurrence is certain, as though it had actually occurred. (داخرين) is a ḥāl.
(وَتَرَى الْجِبالَ تَحْسَبُها جامِدَةً وَهِيَ تَمُرُّ مَرَّ السَّحابِ): the wāw is a conjunction; (ترى الجبال) is an imperfect verb in the nominative, a latent agent whose implied form is "you", and a direct object; the seeing is visual. The clause (تحسبها) is a ḥāl of (الجبال); the hāʾ is the first object of (تحسبها) and (جامدة) its second object. In (وهي) the wāw is circumstantial and (هي) is a mubtadaʾ, the clause (تمر) is the khabar, and the clause is a ḥāl of (جامدة). [Translator's note: the source does not parse (مر السحاب), a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and muḍāf ilayhi.] (صُنْعَ اللَّهِ الَّذِي أَتْقَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ إِنَّهُ خَبِيرٌ بِما تَفْعَلُونَ): (صنع) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) emphasising the content of the clause before it, the maṣdar (verbal noun) being annexed to its agent; (الذي) is an adjective of (الله), and the clause (أتقن) is the ṣila; (كل شيء) is the object of (أتقن). (إن), its noun and its khabar; (بما) is attached to (خبير), and the clause (تفعلون) is the ṣila of (ما).

* Rhetoric:
In these verses there are several devices, which we summarise as follows:
1- Rational metonymy (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī):
In His words «والنهار مبصرا», seeing is attributed to time, which is not rational. He did not bring the speech as a counterpart of what precedes it, namely «ألم يروا أنا جعلنا الليل ليسكنوا فيه»; rather He made one of them a reason and the other a ḥāl, because the correspondence has been observed from the side of the meaning, since the meaning of «مبصرا» is "so that they may see in it the ways of moving about and earning". This is natural, unaffected composition.
2- Reporting the future with the past:
He reported the future with the past in His words «ففزع من في السموات ومن في الأرض», whereas the context required that He also bring the future; but He turned to the past to convey the certainty of the terror and that it will come to pass without doubt, because the past verb indicates the existence of the act and its being certain.
3- Antithesis (al-ṭibāq):
In His words «وترى الجبال تحسبها جامدة وهي تمر مر السحاب» there is a marvellous antithesis between immobility and rapid motion: He made what appears to the eye of the onlooker like the mountain in its immobility and firmness, yet it is swift, passing at a rapid pace as the clouds pass. This is the way of great bodies of large number: when they move, their movement can scarcely be discerned, as al-Nābigha said, describing an army:
بأرعن مثل الطود تحسب أنهم ... وقوف لحاج والركاب تهملج
(With a towering host like a great mountain, you would think them standing still for some need, while the mounts are trotting swiftly.)
This is a splendid verse. Al-arʿan is the high mountain, and he borrowed it for the army, then likened it to al-ṭawd, which is the huge mountain, to convey exaggeration in great number. Al-ḥāj is a collective noun whose singular is ḥāja; al-rikāb are the riding beasts, having no singular from its own root; al-hamlaja is a smooth, swift gait, an Arabicised Persian word. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: «The himlāj, among the pack-horses — its plural is hamālīj — and its gait is hamlaja; Arabicised Persian.» He says: we fought the enemy with a mighty army; you would think them standing still for some need because of their great number, while their mounts are hastening on.
Al-Zamakhsharī has an eloquent description of these verses, which we cite as follows:
«Look at the eloquence of this speech, the beauty of its composition and arrangement, the firmness of its binding [Translator's note: the source has «إضماده»], the solidity of its explanation, and how each part takes hold of the waist-band of another, as though it were cast in a single casting. For some reason it has disabled the powers and silenced the eloquent tongues. Something like this maṣdar — i.e. «صنع الله» — when it comes after a speech, comes as a witness to its soundness and a proclaimer of its rightness, and that it could only have been as it was. Do you not see His sayings «صنع الله», «وعد الله» and «فطرة الله» — after He marked them, by annexing them to Himself, with the mark of magnification — how He followed them with His sayings «الذي أتقن كل شيء», «ومن أحسن من الله صبغة», «ولا يخلف الله الميعاد» and «لا تبديل لخلق الله»?»

dervis-irab:20-26.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْهُدْهُدَ): «الهدهد» and «الهُداهد» [Translator's note: the source prints «الهدهد» twice without vowels; two vocalizations are presumably meant] is a bird with stripes and many colours; the singular is «هدهدة», «هدهدة» and «هداهدة», and the plural «هداهد» and «هداهيد». They say "more sharp-sighted than a hoopoe", because they claim that it sees water under the ground. «الهدهد» is also any bird that coos, and many pigeons. Its story with Solomon will come in the Benefits section.
(فَمَكَثَ): with ḍamma and with fatḥa on the kāf; the first is of the pattern of qaruba and the second of the pattern of naṣara. In al-Qāmūs and elsewhere: «مكث يمكث», of the pattern of naṣara: makthan, mukthan, mukūthan, makathānan, makkīthā and makkīthāʾ in a place — he stayed and remained; so he is «ماكث», and the noun is «المكث» and «المُكث». «مكُث يمكُث», of the pattern of qaruba, makātha: he stayed and was composed (grave).
(سَبَإٍ): a land situated in the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula, in Yemen, mentioned in the books of the Old Testament and in the works of the Arabs, Greeks and Romans. It possessed a great civilization, and its inhabitants traded in gold, silver and precious stones.
Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: «"Saba'" was read as a triptote and as a diptote, and it has also been transmitted with sukūn on the bāʾ. From Ibn Kathīr, in one transmission, «سبا» with alif, as in their saying "they went off like the hands of Sabā (ayādī sabā)". He is Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān. Whoever makes it the name of the tribe does not inflect it fully; whoever makes it the name of the clan or of the greatest father [Translator's note: the source prints «الأدب الأكبر», evidently for «الأب الأكبر»] inflects it fully. The poet said:
من سبأ الحاضرين مأرب إذ ... يبنون من دون سيله العرما
(Of Sabaʾ, the settled dwellers of Maʾrib, when they built the dam against its torrent.)
And he said:
الواردون وتيم في ذرا سبأ ... قد عض أعناقهم جلد الجواميس
(Those who come to water, and Taym, in the shelter of Sabaʾ — buffalo-hide [straps] have bitten their necks.)
Then the city of Maʾrib was called Sabaʾ — between it and Ṣanʿāʾ is a journey of three [days] — just as Maʿāfir was named after Maʿāfir ibn Udd. It may mean the city or the people.»
The meaning of "they went off like the hands of Sabā":
One says «ذهبوا أيدي سبا», and there are two usages: «أيدي سبا» and «أيادي سبا». It has two treatments: either you compound the two nouns into a single noun and make them indeclinable because they imply the conjunction, as they did with «خمسة عشر»; or, second, you annex the first to the second. Their position is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and what is meant is "they went off dispersed and scattered" and the like. If it is objected that «سبا» is definite, it is answered that compounding them dropped the sense of proper-namehood and they became one noun. The origin of this proverb is that when [the people of] Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān were warned of the Flood of al-ʿArim, they left Yemen dispersed through the lands; so of every group that dispersed it was said: they went off like the hands of Sabā. What is meant by "hands" is the sons and the family, not the bodily limb, since the dispersal befell them; the term "hands" was borrowed because in strength and in the power to strike through them they are like hands.
(الْخَبْءَ): a maṣdar (verbal noun) in the sense of «المخبوء» (the hidden). One says «خبأت الشيء أخبؤه خبئا», of the pattern of nafaʿa, i.e., I concealed it. The khabʾ in the heavens is the rain and in the earth the plants.

* I'rab:
(وَتَفَقَّدَ الطَّيْرَ فَقالَ ما لِيَ لا أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ أَمْ كانَ مِنَ الْغائِبِينَ): resumptive speech, to begin relating another matter that occurred to Solomon during the journey in which the story of the ants took place. «تفقد» is a past verb whose fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, its implied form being "huwa" (he), i.e., Solomon; «الطير» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). «فقال» is conjoined to «تفقد». «ما» is an interrogative noun in the position of nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and «لي» its khabar (predicate); the clause «لا أرى الهدهد» is a ḥāl. «أم» is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿa); «كان» is an incomplete (nāqiṣ) past verb whose noun is a latent pronoun referring to the hoopoe, and «من الغائبين» is the khabar of «كان».
(لَأُعَذِّبَنَّهُ عَذاباً شَدِيداً أَوْ لَأَذْبَحَنَّهُ أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطانٍ مُبِينٍ): the lām paves the way for the oath (muwaṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam); «أعذبنه» is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa because of its connection with the heavy nūn of emphasis; its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā" (I), and the hāʾ is the direct object. «عذابا» is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and «شديدا» an adjective. «أو لأذبحنه» is conjoined to «لأعذبنه», and «أو ليأتيني» is also conjoined to it; «بسلطان» are attached to (mutaʿalliq) «يأتيني», and «مبين» is an adjective.
(فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ فَقالَ أَحَطْتُ بِما لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ وَجِئْتُكَ مِنْ سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ يَقِينٍ): the fāʾ is resumptive; «مكث» is a past verb with a latent agent referring to the hoopoe or to Solomon. «غير بعيد» is an adverb of time attached to «مكث», or, more correctly, an adjective of an omitted adverb whose place it has taken, i.e., "a time not far" — or "a place not far", in which case it is an adverb of place. «فقال» is conjoined to «مكث», and this supports the pronoun's referring to the hoopoe. The clause «أحطت» is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); «بما» are attached to «أحطت»; the clause «لم تحط» [Translator's note: the source prints «نحط» here] is the ṣila (relative clause), and «به» are attached to «تحط». «جئتك» is conjoined to «أحطت»; «من سبأ» are attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of «نبأ»; «بنبإ» are attached to «جئتك», and «يقين» is an adjective of «نبأ».
(إِنِّي وَجَدْتُ امْرَأَةً تَمْلِكُهُمْ وَأُوتِيَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَلَها عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ): «إن» and its noun; the clause «وجدت امرأة» is the khabar of «إني»; the clause «تملكهم» is an adjective of «امرأة». «وأوتيت»: the wāw is a conjunction or of ḥāl; the clause «أوتيت» is either conjoined to the clause «تملكهم» — the conjoining of a past to an imperfect being permissible because the imperfect has the meaning of the past, i.e., "she ruled them" — or a ḥāl of the agent of «تملكهم», with «قد» implied. «من كل شيء» are attached to «أوتيت», or to an omitted word which is the second object of «أوتيت», the implied sense being likewise "of everything". «لها» is a fronted khabar, «عرش» a postponed mubtadaʾ and «عظيم» an adjective.
(وَجَدْتُها وَقَوْمَها يَسْجُدُونَ لِلشَّمْسِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ): the clause «وجدتها» is a badal (substitute) of «وجدت امرأة», so it falls within the scope of the khabar. «وجدتها» here takes one object, because it means "I met her"; the hāʾ is the direct object, and «قومها» is conjoined to the hāʾ or is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment). The clause «يسجدون» is a ḥāl of its object and what is conjoined to it; «للشمس» are attached to «يسجدون», and «من دون الله» is a ḥāl.
(وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ أَعْمالَهُمْ فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ فَهُمْ لا يَهْتَدُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; «زين» is a past verb, «لهم» are attached to it, «الشيطان» is its agent and «أعمالهم» its object. «فصدهم» is conjoined to «زين», and «عن السبيل» are attached to «صدهم». «فهم»: the fāʾ is a conjunction, «هم» a mubtadaʾ and the clause «لا يهتدون» its khabar.
(أَلَّا يَسْجُدُوا لِلَّهِ الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الْخَبْءَ فِي السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ): the nūn must be omitted in writing, following the practice of the Muṣḥaf. «أن» is a maṣdariyya particle that makes the verb accusative, and «لا» is redundant (zāʾida); the meaning is «أن يسجدوا». This interpreted maṣdar is governed by His words «لا يهتدون», but by removal of the preposition, namely «إلى»; the meaning is "so they are not guided to prostration". On this i'rab it is not correct to pause at «يهتدون». The maṣdar may also be a badal of «أعمالهم», the implied sense being "Satan adorned for them their deeds: not prostrating"; or it may be a badal of «السبيل». It was also read with «ألا» lightened, in which case it is a particle of alerting and opening; «يا» is a vocative particle, the one addressed being omitted, and «اسجدوا» is an imperative verb. The proper spelling on this reading would have been «يا اسجدوا», but the Companions dropped the alif of «يا» and the hamzat al-waṣl of «اسجدوا» in writing, since they dropped in pronunciation, and joined «يا» to the sīn of «اسجدوا», so its form became «يسجدوا», as you see. Thus the two readings coincide in sound and script and differ in their underlying analysis. The discussion of the grammarians' disagreement over «يا» entering a verb or a particle will come in the Benefits section [Translator's note: no such discussion appears in the Benefits section of this entry]. «لله» are attached to «يسجدوا»; «الذي» is a relative, a naʿt (adjective) of «الله»; the clause «يخرج الخبء» is the ṣila; «في السموات والأرض» are attached to «الخبء», i.e., what is hidden in the heavens; or to «يخرج», «في» having the sense of «من», i.e., He brings it out from the heavens and the earth.
(وَيَعْلَمُ ما تُخْفُونَ وَما تُعْلِنُونَ): «يعلم» is conjoined to «يخرج», so it falls within the scope of the ṣila; the agent of «يعلم» is a latent pronoun referring to Allah; «ما» is a relative, the direct object; the clause «تخفون» is the ṣila, and «ما تعلنون» is conjoined to «ما تخفون».
(اللَّهُ لا إِلهَ إِلَّا هُوَ رَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ): resumptive speech, brought to extol Allah's mighty Throne after the allusion to the throne of Bilqīs — and between the two there is a vast gulf.

* Rhetoric:
Jinās al-taṣrīf (paronomasia by variation):
In His words «وجئتك من سبأ بنبإ يقين» there is jinās al-taṣrīf, which is the difference in the form of two words by replacing one letter with another, either of the same point of articulation or of a nearby point of articulation. It is among the beauties of speech related to wording, on condition that it comes naturally, far from affectation, preserving the soundness of the meaning. Here it came adding to soundness, so it was fine and delicate. Do you not see that had He said «بخبر» instead of «بنبإ», the meaning would have been sound and straight, but it came melodious and sweet in ring because of the agreement of «سبأ» and «نبأ». Its like has preceded in His words in Sūrat al-Anʿām: «وهم ينهون عنه وينأون عنه».

* Benefits:
1- The story of Solomon and the hoopoe:
Following our custom, we give one of the reports mentioned about the story of Solomon and the hoopoe, because of the narrative roots in it and as a preparation for the gifted, inspired writers of stories:
It is related that when Solomon had finished building Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), he prepared for the pilgrimage with his assembled host. He reached the Sanctuary and stayed there as long as he wished, and every day of his stay he offered five thousand she-camels, five thousand cows and twenty thousand sheep. Then he resolved to go to Yemen, and left Mecca in the morning heading toward Canopus (Suhayl). He reached Ṣanʿāʾ at noon and saw a beautiful land resplendent with greenery, so he alighted to take his midday meal and pray, but they did not find water. The hoopoe was his qunāqin, i.e., his guide, and it saw water under the ground as water is seen in a glass, so he looked for it for that reason. When Solomon alighted, the hoopoe soared up and saw another hoopoe perched, so it swooped down to it and described to it the kingdom of Solomon and everything that had been subjected to him. The other told it of the kingdom of Bilqīs, and that under her hand were twelve thousand commanders, and under each commander a hundred thousand, and it went with it to look, and it did not return until after the afternoon prayer. It is mentioned that a ray of sun fell on Solomon's head, so he looked, and the hoopoe's place was empty. He called the chief of the birds, the vulture, and asked him about it, but found he had no knowledge of it. Then he said to the lord of the birds, the eagle: "Bring it to me." The eagle rose into the air until it saw the world like a bowl; then it turned right and left and saw the hoopoe approaching. The eagle swooped down, making for it, and the hoopoe knew that the eagle meant it harm and said: "By the right of the One who strengthened you and gave you power, have mercy on me." So it left it and said: "Woe to you, may your mother be bereaved of you! The Prophet of Allah has sworn to punish you." It said: "And did the Prophet of Allah make no exception?" It said: "Yes, he did; he said: «or he shall bring me a clear authority»." It said: "Then I am saved." When it came near Solomon it let down its tail and wings, trailing them on the ground in humility before Solomon. When it drew close to him, he took hold of its head and pulled it toward him, and it said: "O Prophet of Allah, remember your standing before Allah." Solomon trembled and pardoned it, then asked it: "What kept you from me?" The hoopoe said: «أحطت بما لم تحط به…» to the end.
A point of eloquence:
Al-Zamakhsharī said: «If you say: he swore to one of three things; his swearing to his own two acts is unobjectionable, but how was his swearing to the hoopoe's act valid, and how did he know that it would bring an authority, so that he could say "by Allah, it shall bring me an authority"? I say: when he arranged the three with «أو» in the ruling, namely the oath, his words amounted to your saying "one of these things shall certainly happen"; that is, if the bringing of an authority occurs, there will be no punishment and no slaughter, and if not, one of these two will occur. There is no claim to knowledge in this.»
2- Who was Bilqīs?
Bilqīs was the daughter of Sharāḥīl ibn Abī Sarḥ ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Qays ibn Ṣayghī [Translator's note: so in the source; the name is usually given as Ṣayfī] ibn Sabaʾ. Ibn al-Kalbī said: her father was one of the greatest kings. Her story will come. Al-Ḥarīrī mentioned in Durrat al-Ghawwāṣ that the correct form of the word «بلقيس» is with kasra on the bāʾ, because every foreign word that is Arabized should by analogy be assimilated to the patterns of Arabic speech, and «بلقيس» is accordingly so [i.e., like «فِعليل»].
Among the reports of Sayf al-Dawla: the two Khālidīs praised him, and he sent them a page-boy and a slave-girl, each of them with a purse of money and a chest of clothes from Egypt and Syria. They wrote to him [Translator's note: the poem's lines are broken across lines in the source; they are given here as whole verses with the text unchanged]:
لم يغد شكرك في الخلائق مطلقا ... إلا ومالك في النوال حبيس
(Thanks to you have not gone forth unbounded among people except because your wealth is devoted to giving.)
خولتنا شمسا وبدرا أشرقت ... بهما لدينا الظلمة الحنديس
(You granted us a sun and a full moon, by which the pitch darkness with us has shone.)
رشنأ أتانا، وهو حسنا يوسف ... وغزالة هي بهجة، بلقيس
(A fawn came to us, in beauty a Joseph, and a gazelle who in splendour is a Bilqīs.) [Translator's note: «رشنأ» is as printed, evidently for «رشأ» (fawn).]
هذا ولم تقنع بذاك وهذه ... حتى بعثت المال وهو نفيس
(And you were not content with him and her, but sent wealth as well, and precious it is.)
أتت الوصيفة وهي تحمل بدرة ... وأتى على ظهر الوصيف الكيس
(The slave-girl came carrying a purse, and on the back of the page-boy came the bag.)
وكسوتنا مما أجادت حوكه ... مصر وزادت حسنه تنيس
(You clothed us in what Egypt wove finely and Tinnīs added to in beauty.)
فغدا لنا من جودك المأكول وال ... مشروب والمنكوح والملبوس
(So from your bounty we now have what is eaten, what is drunk, what is wed, and what is worn.)
When Sayf al-Dawla read it, he said: "They did well, except in the word «المنكوح», since it is not among the words with which kings are addressed."
The story of Bilqīs and her smooth palace was a source of inspiration for poets. Al-Buḥturī included all of it in an ode in which he praised al-Mutawakkil and mentioned the building of the famous pool; from it:
يا من رأى البركة الحسناء رؤيتها ... والآنسات إذا لاحت مغانيها
(O you who have seen the beautiful pool — the sight of it, and the fair maidens when its haunts appear,)
بحسبها أنها في فضل رتبتها ... تعدّ واحدة والبحر ثانيها
(it is enough for it that in the excellence of its rank it is counted first and the sea second to it;)
كأن جن سليمان الذين ولوا ... إبداعها فأدقوا في معانيها
(as if the jinn of Solomon had charge of creating it and made its features exquisite;)
فلو تمر بها بلقيس عن عرض ... قالت هي الصرح تمثيلا وتشبيها
(were Bilqīs to pass by it by chance, she would say: "It is the palace," by way of likeness and comparison.)
3- The prostrations of the Qur'an:
In connection with His words «ألّا يسجدوا لله»: Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī agreed that the prostrations of the Qur'an are fourteen; they differed only over the prostration of «ص», which for Abū Ḥanīfa is a prostration of recitation and for al-Shāfiʿī a prostration of thanks, and over the two prostrations of Sūrat al-Ḥajj.
4- The story of the Flood of al-ʿArim and the dispersal of the Arabs "like the hands of Sabā":
We give here some of the related legends for their charm and benefit:
Sabaʾ is the father of the tribes of Yemen who were dispersed from the Dam of Maʾrib, whom Allah tore into utter pieces. He was called Sabaʾ because he was the first to take captives (sabā al-sabī). It has been said that Sabaʾ was the name of their mother and Maʾrib the name of their town. Sabaʾ was among the most beautiful of Allah's lands, the most fertile and the richest in trees and water. Allah mentioned that it was two gardens, on the right and the left. It was a month's journey by a month for the hard-riding traveller, who would travel through gardens from its beginning to its end, never facing the sun and never leaving the shade, with the water flowing, the air clear and the space wide. They remained as long as Allah willed; no king opposed them but they broke him. In early times the torrents used to overrun it, so the king of Ḥimyar gathered the people of his kingdom and consulted them about warding off the torrent. They agreed on digging channels for it to carry it to the sea. He mustered the people of his kingdom until the water was diverted, and he built a dam where the water ran down from the mountains, paving it with stones and iron, and made in it channels for the water the size of a forearm's circumference; when the torrent came, it was distributed through the channels to their gardens and crops in a measure whose benefit reached all of them. Al-Aʿshā mentioned in his poetry that Ḥimyar built it; he said:
رخام بنته لهم حمير ... إذا جاء ماؤهم لم يرم
(Marble that Ḥimyar built for them; when their water came, it did not move.)
وأروى الزروع وأعنابهم ... على سعة ماؤهم قد قسم
(It watered the crops and their vines; their water was apportioned amply.)
فعاشوا بذلك في غبطة ... فحاق بهم جارف منهدم
(So they lived thereby in happiness; then a sweeping, crashing flood overtook them.)
When the kingship came to ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir Muzayqiyāʾ — so called because every night he tore up (yumazziq) a robe, out of pride, lest it be worn by him again or worn by someone else; and it has been said he was so called because he scattered the Azd through the lands — his brother ʿImrān was a soothsayer. A soothsayer woman called Ẓarīfa came to him and told him of the approaching ruin of the dam and the overflow of the torrent, and warned him. So he gathered the people of Maʾrib, made food for them, and told them about the torrent, and they agreed to emigrate. His brother ʿImrān said to them: "I will describe lands to you; choose whichever of them you wish. Whoever of you has far-reaching ambition and a camel that does not bolt, let him go to the ravine of Karūd" — and Hamdān went there. Then he said: "Whoever of you has statecraft and patience in the crises of fortune, let him go to Baṭn Murr" — and Khuzāʿa went there. Then he said: "Whoever of you wants [palms] firmly rooted in the mud that feed in time of drought, let him go to Yathrib of the palms" — and al-Aws and al-Khazraj settled there. Then he said: "Whoever of you wants wine and leaven, command and the conferring of command, let him go to Buṣrā and Sadīr" — which are in the land of Syria — and Ghassān settled there. Then he said: "Whoever of you wants fine garments, noble horses, gold and silver coin (awrāq), let him go to Iraq" — and Mālik ibn Fahm ibn al-Azd went there. Mālik ibn al-Yamān stayed behind among his people until the torrent drove them out; they settled in Najrān and traced their descent to Madhḥij. A group of them entered among Maʿadd, but Maʿadd drove them out after wars, and they settled in the mountains of al-Sharāt on the borders of Syria. When they dispersed through the lands in this way, the Arabs coined the proverb about them, saying: "They went off like the hands of Sabā" (ayday sabā and ayādī sabā).

dervis-irab:89-93.t:
* I'rab:
(مَنْ جاءَ بِالْحَسَنَةِ فَلَهُ خَيْرٌ مِنْها وَهُمْ مِنْ فَزَعٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ آمِنُونَ): resumptive speech, introduced to pave the way for the close of the sūra by summarising the destiny of the doer of good and the doer of evil. (من) is a conditional noun that puts in the jussive, a mubtadaʾ (subject); (بالحسنة) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (جاء), or to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), the bāʾ then being for accompaniment (mulābasa), i.e. he came bearing it. The fāʾ is a linking particle; (له) is a fronted khabar (predicate) and (خير) a postponed mubtadaʾ; (منها) is an adjective of (خير), or attached to it, taking it as an elative (ism tafḍīl). (هم) is a mubtadaʾ; (من فزع) is attached to (آمنون), and (آمنون) is the khabar. (يوم) is an adverb annexed to one like it [i.e. إذ], and it is attached to an omitted adjective of (فزع), i.e. "occurring on that day". It was read with (فزع) annexed to (يومئذ).
(وَمَنْ جاءَ بِالسَّيِّئَةِ فَكُبَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ فِي النَّارِ هَلْ تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا ما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (من) is conditional; (جاء بالسيئة) is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ). The fāʾ is a linking particle entering upon an omitted «قد», i.e. «فقد كبت», so that the apodosis may properly be joined with it. (كبت) is a passive past verb and (وجوههم) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); (في النار) is attached to (كبت); the clause (فكبت) is in the position of the jussive as the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ). (هل) is an interrogative particle; (تجزون) is a passive imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ) by the retention of the nūn, by way of iltifāt (shift of person); the wāw is the nāʾib fāʿil; and the clause is a ḥāl, i.e. "and their faces are cast down, it being said to them: Are you recompensed …?" (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (ما) is the second object of (تجزون); the clause (كنتم) is the ṣila (relative clause); (كان) and its noun, and the clause (تعملون) is its khabar.
(إِنَّما أُمِرْتُ أَنْ أَعْبُدَ رَبَّ هذِهِ الْبَلْدَةِ الَّذِي حَرَّمَها): the clause is the object of an omitted saying, i.e. "Say to them: I have only been commanded". (إنما) is the restraining particle and what it restrains (kāffa wa-makfūfa); (أمرت) is a passive past verb and the tāʾ is the nāʾib fāʿil; (أن أعبد) is in the sense of a maṣdar (verbal noun) that is accusative by removal of the preposition, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (أمرت). (رب) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (هذه) is annexed to (رب); (البلدة) is a badal (substitute) of the demonstrative, and what is meant by it is Mecca, may Allah guard it; (الذي) is a naʿt (adjective) of (رب هذه البلدة), and the clause (حرمها) is the ṣila. (وَلَهُ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ وَأُمِرْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ): the wāw is circumstantial; (له) is a fronted khabar and (كل شيء) a postponed mubtadaʾ; the secret of this ḥāl will come in the Rhetoric section. (أمرت) is conjoined to the first (أمرت), and (أن أكون من المسلمين) is also conjoined to what precedes. (وَأَنْ أَتْلُوَا الْقُرْآنَ فَمَنِ اهْتَدى فَإِنَّما يَهْتَدِي لِنَفْسِهِ): (وأن أتلو) is conjoined to (أن أكون), i.e. "and I have been commanded to recite"; (القرآن) is the direct object. In (فمن) the fāʾ is for drawing a consequence (tafrīʿiyya) and (من) is conditional, a mubtadaʾ; (اهتدى) is a past verb in the position of the jussive as the protasis; the fāʾ is a linking particle; (إنما) is kāffa wa-makfūfa; (يهتدي) is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "he"; the fāʾ is a linking particle; (إنما) is kāffa wa-makfūfa; (يهتدي) is an imperfect verb in the nominative whose agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; (لنفسه) is attached to (يهتدي). [Translator's note: the source repeats the parsing of «فإنما يهتدي» twice; translated as written.] (وَمَنْ ضَلَّ فَقُلْ إِنَّما أَنَا مِنَ الْمُنْذِرِينَ): conjoined to the preceding clause and parallel to it in its parsing; a verb of request must be supplied after the fāʾ, i.e. "then say to him: I am only one of the warners". (وَقُلِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ سَيُرِيكُمْ آياتِهِ فَتَعْرِفُونَها وَما رَبُّكَ بِغافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (قل) is an imperative verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; (الحمد) is a mubtadaʾ and (لله) the khabar, and the clause is the object of saying (maqūl al-qawl). In (سيريكم) the sīn is a particle of the future; (يريكم) is an imperfect verb, the kāf is the first direct object and (آياته) the second direct object; the clause is part of the completion of the object of saying, falling within its thread. In (فتعرفونها) the fāʾ is a conjunction, and (تعرفونها) is an imperfect verb, an agent and a direct object. The wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is the Ḥijāzī negative; (ربك) is its noun; in (بغافل) the bāʾ is a redundant preposition and (غافل) is genitive in wording and accusative in position because it is the khabar of (ما); (عما) is attached to (غافل), and the clause (تعملون) is the ṣila.

* Rhetoric:
Guarding (al-iḥtirās):
In the saying of the Exalted «وله كل شيء» there is a fine iḥtirās. Mention of this device has preceded, and that it is brought to ward off a misconception that the speech might give rise to. He, Glorified is He, annexed His name to Mecca to honour it and mention its sanctity; and since He annexed His name to the town singled out with this honour, He followed that by annexing everything else to His dominion, to cut off the misconception that His dominion is restricted to the town referred to, and to draw attention to the fact that the first annexation was meant only for honouring, not because it alone is the dominion of Allah the Exalted.
Al-Bāqillānī analyses Sūrat al-Naml:
Furthermore, at the close of this sūra we would like to make a quick, analytical reference to the book «Iʿjāz al-Qur'an» by Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, whose fame has spread among people. It combines with its theological (kalām) spirit a literary character, since in treating inimitability he did not restrict himself to studying it from the theological side, but addressed the aspect of eloquence and style. The orator al-Bāqillānī grew up skilled in disputation, of high standing in the sciences of the Qur'an, the Sunna and theology; he confronted many opponents and dissenters and battled them with proofs, and he debated the scholars of the Byzantines, which aroused the admiration of his contemporaries for him.
The king ʿAḍud al-Dawla sent him to the king of the Byzantines in the year 371 AH on an official embassy. Once, while he was in the Byzantine capital, they brought him in to some priests, and the Qāḍī said to the priest: "How are you, and your wife and children?" The Byzantine was astonished and said to him: "The one who sent you mentioned in the letter of credence that you are the tongue of the community and foremost among the scholars of the religion; did you not know that the metropolitans and monks are above having wives and children?" The Qāḍī Abū Bakr answered him: "We have seen that you do not hold Allah, Glorified is He, above having a wife and children; are the metropolitans with you holier, more majestic and more exalted than Allah, Glorified is He?" The chief of the Byzantines wanted to disgrace the Qāḍī, so he said to him: "Tell me about the story of ʿĀʾisha, the wife of your Prophet, and what was said about her." He answered him: "They are two women about whom was said what was said: the wife of our Prophet and Mary the mother of the Messiah. As for the wife of our Prophet, she did not give birth; and as for Mary, she came with a child carrying him on her shoulders; and Allah declared both of them innocent of what they were accused of." The Byzantine was silenced and could give no answer.
Summary of al-Bāqillānī's theory of inimitability:
1- He begins by presenting the idea in a simple presentation: he establishes the soundness of the text of the Qur'an we have in our hands, that it is truly the Book of Allah revealed to His Prophet, and that it is Muḥammad's sign and his everlasting miracle.
2- He establishes the incapacity of the Arabs to produce its like despite its challenging them repeatedly.
3- From the preceding premises he arrives at a general conclusion which is the summary of his theory of inimitability, namely «the departure of the composition (naẓm) of the Qur'an from all the speech of the Arabs and their compositions». He then explains this theory in the book of inimitability, saying: «The third aspect is that it is novel in composition, marvellous in arrangement, reaching the utmost in eloquence through the variety of its aspects and the diversity of its ways, departing from what is familiar in the composition of all their speech, differing from what is customary in the arrangement of their discourse; it has a style peculiar to it and is distinguished in its sections from the styles of ordinary speech.»
Before entering into the composition of the Qur'an and the analysis of its sūras, he takes up an ode of Imruʾ al-Qays and another of al-Buḥturī, to sketch his method in criticism and the application of his approach. In both odes he moves from the opening to the end, drawing attention to aspects of beauty and points of weakness. In his analysis of the ode of Imruʾ al-Qays — or his Muʿallaqa, more correctly — he weighs what it contains of the arts of expression, variation in speech and composition of discourse against what is similar or close to it in the Qur'an, always drawing attention to the superiority of the Qur'an. Personal criticism often entered into al-Bāqillānī's opinion in analysing the Muʿallaqa of Imruʾ al-Qays, even where that opinion contradicted the opinions of all the critics. Look at him, how he faults the poet in his saying:
إذا قامتا تضوع المسك منهما ...
(When the two of them rose, musk wafted from them …)
He says: «The aspect of affectation in it is his saying "When the two of them rose, musk wafted from them"; had he wished to do well, he would have conveyed that there was fragrance about them in every state; as for only in the state of rising, that is a shortcoming.» This is an evident prejudice by Abū Bakr against the poet and the meaning he treated; for there is no doubt that in this expression there is a fine artistic touch resting on the word «قامتا», because it is the source of motion and life in the whole picture: it shows you the two girls coming and going, their thin garments giving off perfume which spreads through their sides, and the air becomes fragrant with its scent from what motion stirs in the air, carrying the perfume to the noses to inhale it; and that is not possible in sitting and stillness. Nevertheless, we do not deny some of the slips in the creed [Translator's note: so in the source, «العقيدة»; the context suggests «القصيدة», "the ode"] to which al-Bāqillānī drew attention; rather we adopt his opinion and appreciate his depth and fine deduction. Listen to this marvellous criticism that silences tongues. He took up the opening of the Muʿallaqa in the first two verses, which are:
فقا نبك من ذكرى حبيب ومنزل ... بسقط اللوى بين الدخول فحومل
فتوضح فالمقراة لم يعف رسمها ... لما نسجتها من خبوب وشمائل
(Halt, you two, let us weep at the remembrance of a beloved and an abode at the edge of the sand-dune between al-Dakhūl and Ḥawmal, and Tūḍiḥ and al-Miqrāt — its traces not effaced, for what the south and north winds have woven over it.)
And he said: «He was not content with mentioning one boundary until he had defined it by four boundaries, as if he wanted to sell the abode and feared that, if he omitted a boundary, his sale would be invalid or his condition void.»
In his analysis of al-Buḥturī's ode there are some artistic niceties in criticism, which we summarise as follows:
1- Poetic vision: he pointed to its disorder in al-Buḥturī in his likening the phantom to lightning, in al-Buḥturī's saying:
أهلا بذلكم الخيال المقبل ... فعل الذي نهواه أم لم يفعل
برق سرى من بطن وجرة فاهتدت ... بسناه أعناق الركاب الضلل
(Welcome to that approaching phantom, whether it did what we desire or did not — lightning that travelled by night from the hollow of Wajra, by whose gleam the necks of the straying mounts found their way.)
He said: «He made the phantom like lightning because of the brightness of its night journey»; and in his view the phantom is not to be likened to lightning, because lightning is swift and flashing, while the phantom travels as the breeze travels.
2- Padding (al-ḥashw): it is the excess of wording over the required meaning, and it is a defect in composition.
3- Triteness in the figurative image, such as simile, metaphor or metonymy.
4- Verbal lustre: he sees in some of al-Buḥturī's verses lustre and charm, and sees in others a lack of freshness and lustre.
5- Disorder in meaning: of this is his saying in criticising some verses: «The mention of the censurers ran in a way to which this verse does not connect and with which it does not accord; then what he mentioned of waiting, though pretty in wording, is affected in meaning, because one who stands in the abode does not wait for something, but only stands in grief, humility and bewilderment.» These are the verses the criticism treated:
ما الحسن عندك يا سعاد بمحسن ... فيما أتاه ولا الجمال بمجمل
عذل المشوق وإن من سيما الهوى ... في حيث تجهله لجاج العاذل
ماذا عليك من انتظار متيم ... بل ما يضرك وفقة في منزل إن سيل عيّ عن الجواب فلم يطق ... رجعا فكيف يكون إن لم يسأل
(Beauty in you, O Suʿād, does not do good in what it does, nor does loveliness act kindly. The longing one was blamed — and among the marks of passion, where you do not know it, is the censurer's persistence. What harm to you is the waiting of one enslaved by love — nay, what harms you in a pause at an abode? If he is asked, he is too tongue-tied to answer and cannot reply; so how would it be if he were not asked?)
6- Enjambment (al-taḍmīn): it is a defect known among Arab critics.
7- Departing from the structure of the ancient Arabic ode.
8- Complexity and lack of smoothness in arranging and casting the words, which is a defect in formulation and composition.
9- The opening and its connection with disjunction and conjunction (al-faṣl wal-waṣl).
10- Sharing of meanings between him and other poets, with variation in excellence.
11- The construction and arrangement of the phrase, and its variation between sound and disturbed composition.
Analysis of Sūrat al-Naml:
